stimulus.text: Paraphrase of standard accounts of three sisters agriculture: maize, beans, and squash were planted together in the same field. Tall maize stalks held climbing bean vines. Broad squash leaves spread across the ground below, shading the soil. Together the three crops fed dense, settled populations in eastern North America.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts; see grounding.

stem: The Iroquois lived in settled villages in the Northeast woodlands. Which development best explains how permanent village life was possible there?

options.text: Three sisters agriculture, which sustained dense populations in eastern North America.
The use of horses to plow large fields and transport heavy harvests.
options.misconception: Brings in horses that arrived only with Europeans.

options.text: Year-round hunting of migratory bison herds across the far Great Plains.
options.misconception: Borrows a Plains pattern for a Northeast woodland people.

options.text: Tribute payments collected regularly from neighboring empires, as the Mexica did.
options.misconception: Borrows the Mexica tribute empire for Iroquois villagers.

rationales.A: Three sisters farming gave the eastern woodlands a reliable local food supply, which is what permanent villages need.
rationales.B: Horses arrived with Europeans, long after Iroquois villages were established.
rationales.C: Bison hunting was a Plains pattern, not the basis of Northeast woodland villages.
rationales.D: Tribute empires describe the Mexica, not Iroquois villagers in the Northeast.
rationales.general:
1. Name the need. A permanent village needs food from nearby land, year after year.
2. Name the source. In the eastern woodlands, three sisters farming gave that food.
3. Check the rivals. Horses came later with Europeans, bison belonged to the Plains, and tribute belonged to the Mexica.
4. Match source to place. Only three sisters farming fits a Northeast woodland village.
Remember: to explain a settled village, find the food that stayed in one place.
